problem: Prior R2R agents (Seq2Seq, Speaker-Follower, EnvDrop and similar) concatenate image features with a directional encoding into one high-dimensional vector. They do not explicitly model how scene, object/landmark and direction clues relate to each other, and they rarely use the objects mentioned in instructions, even though those objects carry strong localization signals.
motivation: Navigation instructions contain three kinds of contextual clue that depend on one another. Scene answers 'where am I coarsely'. Object answers 'what is my pose relative to this landmark'. Direction answers 'which way do I act'. In 'With the sofa on your left, turn right into the bathroom and stop', the action is conditioned on the landmark and the scene. Modelling these relations both within and across language and vision should reduce ambiguity and make perception more complete.
key_idea: Two interacting graphs are built at every step. A language attention graph has specialized scene/object/direction contexts as nodes and pairwise relational contexts as edges. A language-conditioned visual graph is built per candidate direction and passes messages among scene, object and direction nodes, gated by those language contexts. The updated nodes then score each action.
insight: Adding object features alone does not help. Model #4 (scene+object+direction, no graph) reaches the same val-unseen SPL of 0.51 as Model #1 (scene+direction only). Objects start to help only once relationship modelling and the textual-visual gating are in place: the full model reaches SPL 0.53, while Model #5 (visual graph without the language graph's connections) gets 0.50. Scene features are essential: dropping them (Model #3) cuts val-unseen SPL to 0.46. Objects mainly act as localization signals. They cut val-unseen trajectory length from 17.05 m (Model #2, graph without objects) to 9.99 m. The SR gain grows with the number of object nouns in the instruction, from +0.000 at 1 object to +0.054 at 9. The models with and without objects are complementary: about 10% of unseen samples are solved only by the full model and about 8% only by Model #2.
method: VLN backbone: Bi-LSTM instruction encoder. An instruction-aware LSTM state h_t takes the previous action's direction encoding and a soft-attended global panoramic feature (36 views of ResNet-152 feature + 128-d heading/elevation encoding), with the previous attended global language context as recurrent input.

Language attention graph, nodes: three independent soft-attentions over the instruction words, queried by h_t, yield specialized scene, object and direction contexts h^s, h^o, h^d. Their average becomes the next step's global context.
Language attention graph, edges: a second-level soft-attention over the words, queried by a Tanh projection of each concatenated pair, yields relational contexts h^sd, h^so, h^od.

Language-conditioned visual graph, node initialization: for each candidate direction i there are a scene node (projected ResNet feature), an object node (36 Faster R-CNN VG object labels mapped to 101 classes, GloVe-encoded, soft-attended with h^o) and a direction node (direction encoding concatenated with the previous step's updated direction node as a temporal link). Each node is element-wise multiplied with its matching specialized language context.

Message passing and node update: pairwise messages are non-linear projections of concatenated node pairs, with weights shared between the send and receive directions. Each message is gated by element-wise product with the matching relational context (h^sd, h^so, h^od) and projected. Each node is updated by adding the summed message to its initial value. A single iteration is used, since more iterations gave similar results.

Action prediction and training: a linear layer over the concatenated [scene; object; direction] updated nodes, followed by softmax over candidates. The loss is λ·IL plus A2C RL, following EnvDrop. Stage 1 trains on the R2R train split. Stage 2 fine-tunes the best-SPL model on EnvDrop speaker-augmented data with environmental dropout. R4R uses stage 1 only.

setting.backbone: Bi-LSTM/LSTM seq2seq agent with language and visual entity graph networks, trained from scratch on frozen ResNet-152 (Places365) image features and Faster R-CNN (Visual Genome) object labels embedded with GloVe
setting.training_data: R2R train split, then self-supervised fine-tuning on EnvDrop speaker-generated augmented data with environmental dropout (scale not stated in paper). For R4R: R4R train only, no augmentation.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 views as ResNet features) + detected object labels per candidate view + heading/elevation encodings

numbers_note: Metrics are printed as fractions in the paper (e.g. 0.57) and converted to 0-100 here. No R4R test results are reported.
results: On R2R test-unseen, single-run, the method reaches SR 55 / SPL 52 / NE 4.75. That is the best SPL and NE among compared methods, above PREVALENT (SPL 0.51, NE 5.30) and AuxRN (SPL 0.51), and +5 SPL over its EnvDrop baseline on both unseen splits. On val-unseen it roughly matches the pre-trained PREVALENT (SR 0.57 vs 0.58, SPL 0.53 each). On R4R val-unseen it improves SDTW from 0.13 (RCM-b fidelity) to 0.34 and nDTW from 0.32 (PTA) to 0.47.
limitations: Objects are used only as additional visual features (GloVe label embeddings over a 101-class vocabulary). They are not used for progress monitoring, instance tracking or reward shaping, and depend on the quality of an external detector.

Gains on R2R val-unseen are on par with, not above, the pre-trained PREVALENT. The models with and without objects solve different subsets (about 10% vs 8% uniquely solved), so neither variant is uniformly better.
Evaluated only in discrete nav-graph Matterport3D (R2R/R4R) with message passing limited to a single iteration.
